text:
A: Hello! Can you hear me?
B: Yes. Hi, I'm Claire.
A: Tereza. Nice to meet you. Sorry, I'm a bit close to the camera.
B: You're fine. Where are you?
A: Leyton, East London. And you?
B: Faversham, in Kent. Little market town. You have a lot of books behind you.
A: Oh, yes. [laughs] Too many. Mostly crime, Scandinavian crime. And some Czech ones, I'm from Brno. I'm in a book club at the library.
B: What are you reading at the moment?
A: For book club it's literary one, about a family in Ireland, it's very slow. Honestly I'm finding it a little bit boring, but I can't say that at book club, everybody loves it.
B: Why can't you say that?
A: Erm... I don't know. I don't want to be the difficult one, I think.
B: You should say it. Book clubs are much better when somebody hates the book. Otherwise it's just everyone nodding over biscuits, you know.
A: [laughs] Maybe. I bring the cake, so maybe they forgive me.
B: Exactly. That's your leverage. What do you do, for work?
A: Clinical trials coordinator, at a hospital. Very organised job, lots of checklists. I plan everything. Even holidays, I have a spreadsheet.
B: God. I'm the opposite. I book things the night before. I once nearly missed a ferry to France because I hadn't checked the kids' passports, and my son's had expired. We were in the queue at Dover, and I was sort of arguing with a man in a booth, and in the end we had to drive to the passport office in Peterborough the next morning. The holiday started two days late.
A: Oh no. That is my absolute nightmare. I would be crying in the car.
B: The kids loved it, actually. They thought it was an adventure. My daughter didn't, she's very tidy, she was furious with me. Rightly.
A: [laughs] Maybe she should do your spreadsheets.
B: She probably will, eventually. Where do you like to go?
A: We went to Porto, me and my husband. And Lake District, walking. And I go home to Brno twice a year.
B: Porto's lovely. I prefer Lisbon, though, honestly. It's scruffier. Porto's a bit too pleased with itself.
A: Oh. Erm, I liked it. But I haven't been to Lisbon, so I can't say.
B: Go, and then tell me I'm wrong. People always say I'm wrong.
A: [laughs] Okay, I will put it in the spreadsheet. Sorry, can I ask, the painting behind you, is it yours?
B: Yes. It's not finished. I've got about six in the spare room in the same state.
A: It's beautiful, the colours. Why don't you finish them?
B: [pause] I don't really know. I think if I finish them I have to decide if they're any good. Which is a bit—
